explanations: luna: The section names rain as رزق and follows it to food; this ayah sends water from the sky, brings forth fruits, and calls them provision for people (رِزْقًا لَّكُمْ). | terra: Water descends from the sky and brings fruits as provision, a direct Qur'anic realization of rain being called rizq.
terra: The sea is parted to save Israel and drown Pharaoh's people before their eyes; one body of water is measured mercy and sweeping judgment.

luna: The section pictures water breaking through stone; here Moses strikes a stone and twelve springs burst from it (فَٱنفَجَرَتْ مِنْهُ ٱثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ عَيْنًا), giving the image a measured communal supply. | terra: Moses strikes the rock, twelve springs burst from it, every people knows its drinking place, and the gift closes with a ban on spreading corruption.

luna: The section's named ف ج ر root is water breaking out through rock; this ayah says some stones let rivers burst from them (يَتَفَجَّرُ مِنْهُ ٱلْأَنْهَارُ), the exact image it develops. | terra: Stone can gush rivers, split so water emerges, or fall in awe; this is the section's exact reversal of hearts harder than rock and rock opened by water.
terra: Water from heaven revives earth after death, while winds and clouds are directed between heaven and earth; it sets the complete ordered water system as a sign.

luna: The section says فساد grows and things leave their proper measure; this destroyer spreads فساد on earth and ruins crops and offspring (يُهْلِكَ ٱلْحَرْثَ وَٱلنَّسْلَ), a concrete reversal of rain's yield. | terra: The corruptor destroys crops and offspring, so fasād is shown undoing the living produce that water and earth bring forth.
terra: God contracts and expands and to Him people return, a compact pairing of changing measure with the return that closes the section.
terra: The river is made an explicit test and drinking from it is limited to a small allowance, joining water, measure, and trial in one scene.
terra: A downpour strips the thin soil from a hard rock and leaves it bare, reversing the section's rock that opens to release water and making rain disclose empty action.

luna: The section says measured rain corresponds to measured provision; this parable gives a garden on high ground that yields double after a heavy shower or still yields after a light drizzle, showing productive outcomes at different rain amounts. | terra: A high garden struck by heavy rain gives double produce, yet even light rain suffices; differing amounts of water remain fruitful within their fit measure.
terra: A fruit garden with rivers is struck by a fiery whirlwind at its owner's moment of need, reversing sustained provision into sudden loss.
terra: Former generations received abundant rain and rivers, yet were destroyed for their sins; the same water-given power and later ruin form the section's historical current.
terra: Those deceived by worldly life receive boiling drink because they disbelieved, opposing water as provision to water as requital.

luna: The section's rain becomes plants and fruit; this ayah sends water from the sky, brings out varied growth, grain and clusters of dates, and names its ripe fruit as a sign for reflection. | terra: Water from heaven brings every vegetation, grain, dates, grapes, olives, and pomegranates; looking at fruit and ripening makes provision's growth the sign.
terra: Gardens, dates, crops, olives, and pomegranates are given for eating and due sharing, but waste is forbidden; flourishing provision carries an explicit boundary against excess.
terra: The command to eat and drink but not exceed bounds joins provision and water directly to the moral limit expressed by the section's overflow image.

luna: The section's فساد is what leaves a thing balanced; this ayah forbids فساد on earth after its repair (بَعْدَ إِصْلَاحِهَا), setting destructive overflow against a restored land. Its next ayah, 7:57, supplies the rain and revival scene. | terra: The ban on corrupting earth after it has been set right stands immediately before the rain, fruit, and resurrection scene of 7:57.

luna: The section names rain as حَيَا because it revives earth after death; this ayah sends winds and clouds to dead land, brings forth fruit, then says God brings out the dead in the same way (كَذَٰلِكَ نُخْرِجُ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ). | terra: Wind bears heavy cloud, water descends, fruit comes forth, and dead land models the raising of the dead; it states the full rain-life-return sequence developed in the section.
terra: Good land brings vegetation by its Lord's leave while bad land yields scantily, showing differing produce under the same divine signs.
terra: Noah and those with him are saved in the ark while deniers are drowned, so one flood carries mercy and judgment together.
terra: The she-camel is a sign and must be left to feed on God's earth unharmed, giving Thamūd a concrete provision-related limit.

luna: The section's Thamud carve rock at the valley and later increase فساد; Salih recalls their carving of mountain homes (تَنْحِتُونَ ٱلْجِبَالَ بُيُوتًا) and forbids being corruptors (مُفْسِدِينَ), directly joining their settlement and moral excess. | terra: Thamūd is settled in the land, builds on its plains, carves mountain homes, and is told not to roam as corrupters; this directly reunites rock dwelling and fasād.
terra: They hamstring the she-camel and defiantly demand punishment, openly crossing the limit set in 7:73.
terra: The earthquake leaves them fallen in their homes, completing the fall of those settled in and carving the land.

luna: The section contrasts the cloud expected to bring rain with a painful punishment and describes punishment poured from above; this ayah says Lot's people were rained upon (وَأَمْطَرْنَا عَلَيْهِم مَّطَرًا), a rain-word used for destruction rather than drink or growth. | terra: A punitive rain falls on Lot's people, making rain itself the vehicle of the criminals' end rather than of life.
terra: Pharaoh's people are seized with years of drought and diminished fruits so they might remember, making restricted provision a sign rather than humiliation.
terra: They claim good provision as their due and treat hardship as an omen from Moses, closely matching the human error of reading provision as a status verdict.
terra: The flood is among the detailed signs sent against Pharaoh's arrogant criminal people, joining tyranny with literal overwhelming water.

luna: The section groups Pharaoh with those who exceeded limits and received punishment; here his people are drowned in the sea (فَأَغْرَقْنَٰهُمْ فِى ٱلْيَمِّ), making water itself the judgment. | terra: After denying the signs, Pharaoh's people are drowned in the sea; the destructive water is expressly tied to their heedlessness.

luna: The section's rock-to-water image recurs when Moses strikes the rock and twelve springs gush (فَٱنۢبَجَسَتْ مِنْهُ); each group knows its drinking place, linking the release to allotted provision. | terra: The struck rock bursts into twelve springs and each tribe knows its watering place, tying gushing provision to an apportioned communal measure.
terra: The people are tested with good things and bad things so they may return, another explicit denial that ease or restriction alone fixes divine status.
terra: The rejecters ask for stones to be rained from heaven or painful punishment if the message is true, perversely requesting punishment in rain's place.
terra: Disbelievers receive a drink of boiling water and painful punishment, joining punitive liquid explicitly with ʿadhāb.
terra: Worldly life is water from heaven mingling with earth's growth until people think they command it, when a divine command leaves it mown; abundance never proves ownership.
terra: Noah's party is saved in the ark, made successors, and the deniers are drowned; destructive water also opens a renewed human life.

luna: The section names Pharaoh with the tyrants beneath the poured scourge; this ayah shows Pharaoh overtaken by drowning in the sea (أَدْرَكَهُ ٱلْغَرَقُ), a water-borne punishment in his own story. | terra: Israel crosses the sea and Pharaoh pursues until drowning overtakes him, making his moral excess end in literal overwhelming water.

luna: The section's Noah flood has an onset marked by the oven boiling over (فَارَ ٱلتَّنُّورُ); 54:12 then depicts earth bursting into springs, so this ayah adds the deluge's first signal. | terra: The oven gushes at the arrival of the command and Noah is told to load the ark, making a bursting source the threshold of the flood.

luna: The section recalls Noah's flood; here the ark moves amid waves like mountains (فِى مَوْجٍ كَٱلْجِبَالِ), making the scale of the flood visible. | terra: The ark moves through mountain-like waves, showing the destructive scale reached when water leaves its ordinary bounds.

luna: In Noah's flood, a wave separates his son from the ark and he drowns; this gives the section's water-overflow scene a human consequence beyond the meeting of waters in 54:12. | terra: Noah's son seeks refuge on a mountain but is separated by a wave and drowned, showing that height cannot master the decreed flood.

luna: The section recalls Noah's flood as earth bursting into springs; at its close God commands earth to swallow its water and sky to stop (ٱبْلَعِى مَآءَكِ وَيَٰسَمَآءُ أَقْلِعِى), placing a boundary on overflow. | terra: Earth is commanded to swallow its water and sky to withhold, after which the water subsides; the flood is returned to bounds by paired commands below and above.

luna: Hud tells Ad that turning back would bring rain pouring abundantly (يُرْسِلِ ٱلسَّمَاءَ عَلَيْكُم مِّدْرَارًا); alongside the section's cloud that Ad mistakes for rain but receives as punishment, this shows the same sky's merciful alternative. | terra: Hūd promises his people abundant rain and added strength if they seek forgiveness, so the people who mistook punishment for rain are also offered rain as mercy.
terra: The she-camel is called God's sign and must be left to feed unharmed, another formulation of the boundary Thamūd violates.

luna: The section says punishment is poured down from above and recalls Ad's expected rain; in Lot's destruction this ayah specifies that stones of baked clay are rained upon the overturned towns (وَأَمْطَرْنَا عَلَيْهَا حِجَارَةً), making precipitation itself the punishment. | terra: The overturned towns receive a rain of layered baked stones, a descending judgment opposed to the water that opens earth for crops.
terra: Full measure and weight are commanded together with a ban on spreading corruption in the land, joining balance and fasād explicitly.
terra: Seven years of diligent cultivation and stored grain show abundant produce being measured against a coming shortage.
terra: Seven severe years consume what was stored, making restriction part of an ordered cycle rather than a verdict of humiliation.
terra: A later year brings relief by rain and renewed pressing of produce, completing the return from scarcity to provision.
terra: Neighboring plots, vineyards, crops, and palms are watered with one water yet differ in produce, showing that measured difference is divine ordering rather than disgrace.
terra: After describing increase and decrease in the womb, the ayah says everything with God is by measure; the connection is the same governing qadar, not a water scene.

luna: The section's w-d-y lexicon calls a valley a channel for a flood; here valleys run according to their capacity (سَالَتْ أَوْدِيَةٌ بِقَدَرِهَا), while swelling foam vanishes and what benefits people remains. | terra: Rain makes valleys flow according to their measure, while the flood carries swelling foam; this directly gathers the section's valley-channel, overflow, measure, and passing-foam image.

luna: The section says a person mistakes narrowed رزق for humiliation; this ayah says God expands and restricts provision, then contrasts worldly rejoicing with the smallness of this life beside the Hereafter. | terra: God expands and restricts provision, while people rejoice in the nearer life that is only slight beside the Hereafter; this directly corrects the human reading in 89:16.
terra: Hell gives the obstinate tyrant foul water to drink, turning water from sustaining gift into punishment.
terra: He tries to swallow it as death comes from every side without ending him, intensifying the boundary between life-giving drink and punitive liquid.
terra: God sends water from heaven, brings fruits as provision, and subjects rivers, linking descending water, food, and flowing channels.

luna: The section defines the wadi as a flood channel; Abraham describes settling his descendants in an uncultivated valley (بِوَادٍ غَيْرِ ذِى زَرْعٍ) and asks God for fruit, a specific dry-valley counterpart to the flood-bearing valley and its measured yield. | terra: Abraham settles his family in an uncultivated valley and asks that they be provided with fruits, bringing valley, absent growth, and hoped-for rizq together.
terra: Everything grown in the spread earth is set in due balance, directly joining vegetation to measure before the measured descent of 15:21.
terra: Livelihoods are placed on earth for humans and for creatures they do not provide for, locating provision within the ordered scene continued in 15:21-22.
terra: Every thing has divine treasuries and descends only بِقَدَرٍ مَّعْلُومٍ, giving the governing rule behind measured rain and restricted provision.
terra: Fertilizing winds precede water sent from the sky for drink, while humans are not its storekeepers; provision descends and remains outside their control.
terra: After the town is overturned, baked stones rain upon it; the downward shower realizes punishment rather than provision.

luna: The section recalls Thamud cutting rock homes in the valley; in the Hijr episode, people carve houses from mountains and feel secure (يَنْحِتُونَ مِنَ ٱلْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا ءَامِنِينَ), making the rock-built safety vulnerable to the punishment that follows. | terra: They carve mountain houses feeling secure, sharpening the section's contrast between engineered rock shelter and an unmastered divine judgment.

luna: The section's rain supplies life and provision; this ayah sends water from the sky for drink and plant growth, placing both needs in one scene. | terra: Water from heaven supplies drink and the vegetation in which livestock pasture, presenting the two recipients of measured rain.

luna: The section follows rain into food and gardens; this continuation says water grows crops, olives, palms, grapes and every kind of fruit (يُنۢبِتُ لَكُم بِهِ ٱلزَّرْعَ), making the provision concrete. | terra: The same water grows crops, olives, dates, grapes, and every fruit, filling out the section's garden-from-rain image.
terra: Water sent from heaven gives life to earth after its death, stating the source dictionary explanation of rain as ḥayā.
terra: A secure town receives abundant provision from every place, then ingratitude makes it taste hunger and fear; abundance and restriction expose response rather than rank.

luna: The section's reading of 89:15–16 treats abundance and restriction as God's measure of provision; this ayah states that the Lord expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it (يَبْسُطُ ٱلرِّزْقَ ... وَيَقْدِرُ). | terra: The Lord expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it, directly repeating the correction to 89:16's interpretation.

luna: The section's opening-word root f-j-r is developed as water breaking out before darkness; this ayah uses al-fajr (ٱلْفَجْرِ) for dawn recitation, preserving the root's opening-of-darkness sense beside the water image.
terra: The unbelievers demand that a spring be made to gush from the earth; it is a direct tafjīr scene, though framed as a coercive demand for a sign.

luna: The section sets human demand for a river-filled garden against divinely given water; these deniers demand a garden with rivers running through it and that a spring be made to burst from the earth (تُفَجِّرَ لَنَا مِنَ ٱلْأَرْضِ يَنۢبُوعًا). | terra: The demanded sign is a date-and-grape garden with rivers forcefully gushed through it, exactly the human demand for controlled abundance recalled by the section.
terra: Pharaoh tries to drive the people from the land, so he and those with him are drowned, joining aggression in the land with water judgment.
terra: The wrongdoers who seek relief receive water like molten metal that scalds faces, turning offered drink into the opposite of refreshment.
terra: The parable begins with two grape gardens surrounded by palms and crops, establishing provision in a cultivated enclosure.
terra: Both gardens yield fully and a river is made to gush between them, giving the abundance its watercourse.
terra: The owner has fruit and boasts of greater wealth and followers, turning water-fed produce into a status claim.
terra: He enters his garden wronging himself and claims it will never perish, showing possession mistaken for permanence.
terra: He is told to answer the garden with “What God willed; no power except through God,” the grateful stance missing from status-based readings of provision.
terra: A reckoning from heaven may leave the garden barren and slippery, reversing the assumed security of its abundance.
terra: A garden's water may sink so deeply that its owner cannot seek it, exposing the fragility of apparent abundance.
terra: The fruit is encompassed and its owner wrings his hands over what he spent, completing the collapse of provision treated as permanent rank.
terra: Worldly life is likened to rain-grown vegetation that becomes wind-scattered dry matter, setting passing growth against the One who retains power.

luna: God tells Moses that Pharaoh has transgressed (إِنَّهُۥ طَغَىٰ); the section's named ṭ-gh-y root links that moral excess to water leaving its measure and also names Pharaoh among the overreaching rulers. | terra: Moses is commanded to go to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, naming the same ruler and the same moral overflow as surah 89.
terra: Moses and Aaron are jointly sent to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, repeating the prophetic stance toward that overflow.

luna: The section traces water to living growth; this ayah says God sends water from the sky and brings out diverse kinds of plants (أَزْوَٰجًا مِّن نَّبَاتٍ شَتَّىٰ). | terra: Earth is made a bed with paths, water descends, and diverse plants are brought out, joining habitable ground, channels, and provision.

luna: The section's plant growth is a provision; the continuation tells people to eat and pasture their livestock, directly showing the crop's use. | terra: Humans eat and pasture livestock from that growth, identifying the rain scene's practical provision.
terra: Moses is commanded to strike a dry path through the sea without fearing pursuit or drowning, showing water held back for rescue.
terra: Pharaoh follows and the sea covers his force, so the restrained water returns as judgment upon the transgressor.
terra: Israel is told to eat the good provisions and not transgress in them lest wrath descend, precisely joining rizq, overflow, and punishment from above.
terra: Every living thing is made from water, giving the widest statement of the section's claim that water within its order gives life.
terra: Every soul returns after being tested with bad and good as trial, supporting the section's correction that either form of provision is an examination.

luna: The section links rain-revived earth to the raising of the dead; this ayah describes dead earth stirring, swelling and sprouting after rain (ٱهْتَزَّتْ وَرَبَتْ وَأَنۢبَتَتْ) before likening resurrection to it. | terra: Rain makes lifeless earth stir, swell, and grow every lovely pair, giving a bodily scene for resurrection through water.
terra: Boiling water يُصَبُّ مِن فَوْقِ رُءُوسِهِمْ is poured from above their heads, a precise punitive reversal of rain using the section's pouring verb.

luna: The section names ق د ر for rain descending by measure; this ayah says water came down by measure (بِقَدَرٍ) and was settled in earth, while God remains able to take it away. | terra: Water descends from heaven بِقَدَرٍ, is lodged in the earth, and can be taken away; the ayah states the section's life-giving water held to measure and divine control.
terra: With measured water God produces date-and-grape gardens containing abundant fruits, so measure culminates in janna and food.
terra: The parallel Noah account again makes the gushing oven the signal to embark, directly joining erupting water to a measured divine command.
terra: The question asks whether wealth and children are being hurried to people as good, exposing the same misreading of expanded provision.
terra: بَل لَّا يَشْعُرُونَ denies their perception, confirming that material increase is not a transparent divine verdict.

luna: The section's Ad mistake turns a cloud taken for rain into painful wind; this ayah describes clouds joined and spread until rain and hail descend, showing the actual rain-bearing face of such clouds. | terra: Clouds are driven, joined, and heaped before rain emerges, while hail may strike or be turned away; the same sky-bearing form holds measured benefit and harm.
terra: Every creature is created from water before differing forms of movement are named, extending water's life-giving role beyond revived soil.
terra: God creates everything and determines it with exact determination, supporting the section's claim that water's effects are governed rather than accidental.
terra: Noah's people are drowned for denying the messengers and made a sign, directly linking the flood to the section's procession of past peoples.

luna: This begins the water scene completed in 25:49: winds come as heralds of mercy and God sends pure water from the sky (مَاءً طَهُورًا), supplying the rain whose revival and drink the next ayah describes. | terra: Winds herald mercy and pure water is sent from the sky, the beneficent cloud-scene opposite ʿĀd's fatal expectation.

luna: The section makes rain a provision that revives the earth; this ayah says water is sent to revive dead land and give drink to many people and animals (نُّسْقِيَهُۥ مِمَّا خَلَقْنَآ أَنْعَٰمًا وَأَنَاسِىَّ كَثِيرًا). | terra: The pure water revives a dead land and gives drink to animals and many people, joining life and apportioned sustenance.

luna: After 25:49's reviving rain, this ayah says God distributes the water among people so they may remember, while many refuse; it adds the human response to the provision the section says people misread. | terra: The life-giving water is distributed among people so they may remember, but most respond with ingratitude; distribution and moral response are both measured.

luna: The section points out that عَذَاب shares its named root with عَذْب, pleasant fresh water; this ayah sets fresh sweet water (عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ) against salty bitter water, sharpening the section's turn from expected drink to punishment. | terra: One sea is عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ, sweet and pleasant, and the other salty and bitter, with a barrier between; it gives the exact sweet-water sense placed beside ʿadhāb in the source.
terra: The human being is created from water and given relations of lineage and marriage, another specific expansion of water into living continuity.
terra: The sea splits after Moses strikes it and each part stands like a huge mountain, an immense counterpart to rock splitting for springs.
terra: Moses and his companions are saved, then the others are drowned; the same divided water distinguishes mercy from punishment.
terra: Noah and those with him are saved in the laden ark, identifying the vessel that survives the overwhelming water.
terra: Those remaining are drowned afterward, completing the ark scene's division between rescue and sweeping judgment.
terra: ʿĀd is reminded that cattle and children were supplied to them, setting their strength inside bestowed provision.

luna: The section names Ad among those whose excess brings punishment; this reminder says Ad had gardens and springs (فِى جَنَّٰتٍ وَعُيُونٍ), showing the land and water abundance they received before their downfall. | terra: Gardens and springs complete the provision given to ʿĀd, making the people who mistake a cloud for rain prior recipients of water abundance.
terra: Hūd fears for them the punishment of a tremendous day, placing warning beside the gardens and springs they treat without due response.
terra: Thamūd's security includes gardens and springs, placing cultivated water immediately before the rock houses of 26:149.
terra: Crops and tender date clusters specify what those springs sustain in Thamūd's land.

luna: The section says Thamud carved rock in a valley; Salih addresses the same people as mountain-house cutters (تَنْحِتُونَ مِنَ ٱلْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا), giving the repeated carving scene its own warning context. | terra: Thamūd carves houses from mountains with confident skill, the closest parallel to cutting rock in the valley.
terra: The she-camel has one drinking share and the people another on a known day, placing Thamūd's conduct under a precise water measure.
terra: The people are forbidden to harm the she-camel lest punishment seize them, defining the boundary around the measured drinking share in 26:155.
terra: They hamstring her and become regretful, recording the act that violates the water covenant.
terra: Punishment seizes them after the violation, completing measured water, transgression, and judgment as one sequence.
terra: The rain upon the warned people is called an evil rain, explicitly marking the reversal of the cloud's expected gift.
terra: The command to give full measure begins a passage that opposes quantitative injustice to corruption.
terra: Weighing with an even balance supplies the equilibrium whose loss the section hears in fasād.
terra: Diminishing people's goods and roaming earth as corrupters makes violated measure a form of fasād.
terra: The punishment of the day of shadow-cloud seizes Shuʿayb's people, another reversal in which an overhead form associated with shelter or rain bears destruction.
terra: Solomon calls an extraordinary gift his Lord's favor testing whether he will be grateful, providing the right reading of bestowed abundance.
terra: Nine men in the city spread corruption rather than set things right, supplying the organized fasād of Thamūd behind the rock-city's end.
terra: Their houses lie empty because of wrongdoing, making the carved dwelling itself the remnant of a community that exceeded its bounds.

luna: The section's rain scene can turn from expected gift to punishment; this ayah describes the rain on Lot's people and calls it an evil rain (فَسَآءَ مَطَرُ ٱلْمُنذَرِينَ), a direct contrary use of the same weather image. | terra: An evil rain falls on those who were warned, again placing chastisement in the form normally awaited as mercy.
terra: The question contrasts God, who sends water and grows splendid gardens, with humans who cannot grow their trees; garden provision exposes the true agent.
terra: Pharaoh exalts himself in the land, divides its people, and is called one of the corrupters, specifying the political overflow behind his place in surah 89.
terra: At Midian Moses finds a community watering its flocks and two women holding theirs back, staging water as a scarce and socially apportioned resource.
terra: Moses waters for the women and then declares his need for whatever good God sends, linking the act of giving water to dependence upon provision.
terra: Pharaoh and his hosts are seized and flung into the sea, a concrete water-ending for the ruler listed among the section's overflowers.
terra: Qarun's treasure and exultation establish expanded provision as a test that he reads as personal distinction.
terra: Qarun is told to seek the Hereafter with what God gave, keep a worldly share, and not seek corruption on earth; provision is bounded by moral use.
terra: Qarun claims his wealth was given because of knowledge he possesses, stating the ownership error behind status readings of provision.
terra: Qarun and his house are swallowed by the earth, abruptly removing the wealth whose increase seemed to certify favor.
terra: After Qarun's collapse, observers recognize that God expands and restricts provision; their revised judgment supplies the correction the section demands.
terra: The final home is for those who seek neither elevation nor corruption on earth, opposing both vertical pride and imbalance.
terra: The flood seizes Noah's people while they are wrongdoers, making overwhelming water the concrete consequence of moral transgression.
terra: Several peoples are seized by different consequences of sin, including storm, earth-collapse, and drowning; the catalog marks judgment as fitted rather than uncontrolled nature.
terra: God expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it, another direct formulation of provision's variable measure.

luna: The section's rain is what revives the earth; this ayah asks who sends water from the sky and gives life to dead land, then names God's answer, a repeated formulation of that sign. | terra: Asked who sends water and thereby revives dead earth, the addressees must answer God; control of life-giving rain cannot be inferred from human status.

luna: The section says life is rain that revives land; this ayah joins lightning that inspires fear and hope to water from the sky that revives the earth after death, holding threat and mercy together. | terra: Lightning brings fear and hope, water descends from heaven, and dead earth lives; expected rain is held between promise and danger.
terra: The addressees are asked whether they see God expanding and restricting provision, treating those changes as signs rather than ranks of honor.

luna: The section glosses ف س د as departure from balance and makes the land's and sea's excess audible in that corruption; this ayah says فساد has appeared on land and sea (فِى ٱلْبَرِّ وَٱلْبَحْرِ) through people's deeds, grounding the image in its consequences. | terra: Corruption appears on land and sea through human deeds, giving the section's imbalance a literal terrestrial and maritime spread.

luna: The section's cloud carries either rain or punishment; this ayah depicts God driving clouds, spreading them and bringing rain out of them, the rain-bearing scene that 30:50 calls a trace of mercy. | terra: Winds raise and spread clouds, rain comes through them, and people rejoice when it reaches whom God wills; the ayah stages the cloud's true merciful face.
luna: Before the rain in 30:48, people had been in despair; this makes the section's unexpected rain and its opposite, the cloud that becomes punishment, a specific contrast of expectation.

luna: The section names rain حَيَا for restoring earth after death; this ayah tells the reader to look at the traces of God's mercy in rain and at how He revives earth after its death (يُحْىِ ٱلْأَرْضَ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَآ). | terra: The hearer is commanded to look at the effects of mercy in earth's revival, which is then made evidence for reviving the dead.
terra: Water descends from the sky and causes every noble kind to grow, tying downward water to ordered and valued vegetation.
terra: Water is driven to barren land and crops emerge for livestock and people to eat, a direct scene of hidden provision becoming visible.
terra: Saba has two gardens, is told to eat its Lord's provision, and is given a good land and forgiving Lord; garden growth and rizq are joined before the flood.
terra: The flood of the dam replaces Saba's two fruitful gardens with bitter produce, showing water past its bound sweeping away the provision water had sustained.
terra: The spoiled gardens are requital for ingratitude, locating the loss of watery abundance in response rather than in an automatic verdict of humiliation.
terra: The affluent boast that greater wealth and children exempt them from punishment, stating the false status inference implicit in “my Lord honored me.”
terra: The answer is that God expands and restricts provision, but most people do not know; abundance therefore cannot certify favor.
terra: The Lord expands and restricts provision, and whatever is spent is replaced; measured rizq is paired with trust in its giver.

luna: The section's rain revives dead earth; this ayah describes winds driving clouds to a dead land and God reviving earth after its death, a repeated direct formulation. | terra: Winds raise cloud, cloud is driven to dead land, and earth revives; the ayah then identifies this as the resurrection.

luna: The section notes the shared dictionary root between عَذَاب and عَذْب; this ayah contrasts fresh sweet water (عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ) with salty water, giving the sweet-water side of that lexical turn. | terra: The two seas are explicitly unequal: one is عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ and easy to drink, the other salty and bitter, making sweetness a bounded water quality.
terra: Dead earth is revived and yields grain people eat, making life and food the paired effects of water's hidden work.

luna: The section links a spring to water bursting forth; here God makes springs gush within the earth (فَجَّرْنَا فِيهَا مِنَ ٱلْعُيُونِ) amid gardens of palms and grapes, showing the same release as cultivated abundance. | terra: Gardens of dates and grapes are made and springs are burst within them, explicitly linking janna and tafjīr.
terra: People eat the garden's fruit although their hands did not make it, challenging possession-based readings of provision.
terra: The people of hell receive a mixture of boiling water, a punitive liquid counterpart to the mixed cup of the righteous.
terra: The ayah places those who spread corruption on earth against the God-fearing and names the opposite party ٱلْفُجَّارِ, directly meeting both secondary roots developed in the section.
terra: God sends water down, channels it as springs in the earth, brings varied crops, then they yellow and become debris; the full course shows what flows, flourishes, and passes.

luna: The section rejects reading restricted provision as humiliation; this ayah asks whether people know God expands or restricts provision as He wills, identifying the same measure as a sign. | terra: The question asks whether people know God expands and restricts provision; the changes are signs for believers.
terra: God shows signs and sends provision from the sky; the wording directly supports the section's reading of descending rain as rizq.
terra: They are dragged through boiling water and then burned in fire, making water itself part of chastisement.
terra: Earth's sustenance is apportioned in four days for those who ask, extending measured provision from rain to the created world's food supply.
terra: A furious wind gives ʿĀd a humiliating punishment in worldly life, distinguishing actual humiliation from the imagined humiliation of restricted provision.

luna: The section's rain makes dead ground live; this ayah shows humbled land becoming stirred and growing when water falls, then calls that revival a sign of God's power to revive the dead. | terra: The humbled earth stirs and swells when water descends, and its reviver is declared able to revive the dead.
terra: The One owning heaven's and earth's keys expands and restricts provision, locating its measure in divine dominion.

luna: The section links water over measure with human excess and measured rain with رزق; this ayah says unlimited provision would make people transgress on earth (لَبَغَوْا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ), while God sends it by measure. | terra: If provision were expanded without limit people would transgress, so God sends it in the measure He wills; this makes moral overflow and measured rizq one claim.

luna: The section turns rain from punishment to mercy and food; this ayah says God sends rain after people despair (مِن بَعْدِ مَا قَنَطُوا) and spreads His mercy, an explicit reversal of the feared cloud. | terra: Rain is sent after people despair and divine mercy is spread, correcting the judgment that delayed or narrowed provision means rejection.

luna: This ayah gives the section's measured-water claim directly: God sends water from the sky by measure (بِقَدَرٍ), revives a dead land, and says people will likewise be brought out. | terra: Water is sent from heaven بِقَدَرٍ, dead land is revived, and human emergence is compared to it; measure, life, and return are explicit together.
terra: When Pharaoh's people provoke divine anger, all are drowned, turning imperial overflow into engulfment by water.
terra: Moses is told to leave the sea calm because the pursuing host will be drowned, showing water deliberately held for a measured judgment.
terra: The drowned host leaves behind gardens and springs, contrasting its former watery provision with the sea that ends its power.
terra: صُبُّوا فَوْقَ رَأْسِهِۦ مِنْ عَذَابِ ٱلْحَمِيمِ explicitly joins pouring from above, punishment, and scalding water in one command.

luna: The section links rain to life returning to the earth; this ayah names water sent from the sky as provision that brings the earth back to life after death (فَأَحْيَا بِهِ ٱلْأَرْضَ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا). | terra: What God sends from heaven is explicitly called رِزْقٍ and revives earth after death, uniting the source's rain-rizq and rain-life dictionary senses.

luna: This is Hud's warning to Ad, the scene that leads to their rain-cloud misreading in 46:24; its contribution is the threatened punishment already rejected before they call the cloud rain. | terra: Hūd warns ʿĀd among the dunes before the cloud appears; it locates 46:24's water expectation in the landscape of the people named by surah 89.

luna: The section's Ad scene turns a cloud they take for rain (هَٰذَا عَارِضٌ مُمْطِرُنَا) into a wind bearing painful punishment (رِيحٌ فِيهَا عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ); the expected sweet water and actual scourge occupy one scene. | terra: ʿĀd sees a cloud advancing toward its valleys and calls it rain, but it is the hastened wind containing painful punishment: the expected sweet water becomes chastisement.
terra: The wind destroys everything by its Lord's command until only dwellings remain, completing 46:24's reversal from expected raincloud to erasing judgment.
terra: The promised garden has rivers of unspoiled water and other drinks, while the opposing people drink boiling water that cuts their bowels; provision and punishment share a liquid form.

luna: The section moves from rain to its food and garden yield; this ayah calls the water blessed (مَآءً مُّبَٰرَكًا) and says it brings forth gardens and grain, tying rain directly to produce. | terra: Blessed water descends from the sky and grows gardens and harvested grain, directly realizing water poured down as provision.

luna: The section's rain-to-garden image continues in this ayah's tall date palms with clustered fruit (نَّخْلٍ بَاسِقَٰتٍ لَّهَا طَلْعٌ نَّضِيدٌ), a concrete growth from rain-fed land. | terra: Tall date palms with layered clusters specify the garden growth produced by the blessed water in 50:9.

luna: The section connects rain, رزق and life's return; this ayah calls the crops provision for servants and says the same rain revives dead land (رِّزْقًا لِّلْعِبَادِ وَأَحْيَيْنَا بِهِۦ بَلْدَةً مَّيْتًا). | terra: The crop is provision for servants, dead land is revived with water, and خروج is the likeness for resurrection; growth, rizq, life, and emergence meet explicitly.

luna: The section names the dictionary usage of rain as رزق; this ayah locates people's provision in the sky (وَفِى ٱلسَّمَاءِ رِزْقُكُمْ), making the rain/provision link explicit. | terra: وَفِى ٱلسَّمَاءِ رِزْقُكُمْ locates provision in the sky, supporting the source dictionary claim that rain can be called rizq.
terra: Pharaoh and his forces are seized and cast into the sea while he is blameworthy, giving the surah 89 tyrant a direct water judgment.
terra: The wind sent against ʿĀd is explicitly barren, a precise opposite to the fertilizing rain-bearing wind.
terra: That wind leaves whatever it touches like decayed matter, completing the reversal from water-fed flourishing to desiccation.
terra: Noah's earlier people are called more unjust and more transgressive, joining the moral root specifically to the people destroyed by flood.

luna: This opens the flood scene continued by the section's cited 54:12: the sky's gates are opened with pouring water (بِمَآءٍ مُّنْهَمِرٍ), supplying the downpour that meets the earth's springs. | terra: The gates of heaven are opened with pouring water, supplying the upper half of the flood whose earth-springs meet it in 54:12.

luna: This is the section's own flood formulation: God makes the earth burst into springs (فَجَّرْنَا ٱلْأَرْضَ عُيُونًا), and the waters meet over a matter already decreed, joining eruption to measure. | terra: The earth is burst into springs in وَفَجَّرْنَا ٱلْأَرْضَ عُيُونًا and the two waters meet upon a decreed affair, directly joining gushing with prior measure.
terra: A screaming wind is sent on a day of continuous ill fortune, the punishing answer to ʿĀd's cloud reading.
terra: The wind uproots people like torn palm trunks, replacing the growth expected from rain with uprooting.
terra: Thamūd is told that water is apportioned between them and the she-camel, with each drinking turn attended; measured water becomes the covenant they cross.
terra: Thamūd calls its companion, who takes hold and hamstrings the camel, identifying the breach that follows apportioned water in 54:28.
terra: The question calls attention to the resulting punishment and warnings, turning the broken measure into an admonition.
terra: A single blast leaves them like crushed penwood, completing the destruction triggered after the shared water is violated.
terra: Everything is created بِقَدَرٍ, generalizing the section's measured water and measured provision into a rule of creation.
terra: God raises the sky and sets the balance, supplying the ordered frame for the following prohibition against overflowing the measure.
terra: أَلَّا تَطْغَوْا فِى ٱلْمِيزَانِ forbids overflowing the balance itself, turning the section's water beyond measure into an exact moral rule.
terra: The command to establish weight with justice and not diminish the balance gives the positive form of remaining within measure.
terra: The criminals circulate between hellfire and intensely boiling water, reversing the flowing springs of the gardens in the same surah.
terra: Two gardens are promised to the one who fears standing before the Lord, establishing the setting of the two flowing springs in 55:50.

luna: The section joins a spring and a Garden; this Garden description puts two running springs (عَيْنَانِ تَجْرِيَانِ) among its rewards, pairing water with the garden named at the section's end. | terra: The two promised gardens contain two flowing springs, making moving water internal to janna.
terra: Two further gardens are named before their two gushing springs in 55:66, keeping janna and spring inseparable.

luna: The section's spring image is water forced into a channel; these Gardens contain two bubbling springs (عَيْنَانِ نَضَّاخَتَانِ), a specific gushing-water counterpart in paradise. | terra: Two other gardens contain two gushing springs, a direct non-fajara wording for the section's springing-water scene.
terra: The companions of the right receive poured-out water, a paradise counterpart to water poured as earthly mercy and punishment.
terra: The companions of the left are in scorching wind and boiling water, pairing the two elements that replace merciful wind and rain.
terra: They drink boiling water after eating from the punitive tree, turning food and drink together into judgment.
terra: They drink like desperately thirsty camels, making abundance of drinking unable to satisfy or give life.

luna: The section's spring, rain and sweet-water notes meet the question about the water people drink (ٱلْمَآءَ ٱلَّذِى تَشْرَبُونَ); 56:69–70 continue by asking who sends it and whether it could be made bitter. | terra: The hearer is asked to consider the water being drunk, opening a direct challenge to claims of possession over provision.

luna: The section traces provision to water poured from above; this ayah asks whether people bring their drinking water down from the rain cloud (ءَأَنتُمْ أَنزَلْتُمُوهُ مِنَ ٱلْمُزْنِ) or God does, locating its source with the speaker. | terra: The next question asks whether humans sent it from the raincloud or God did, assigning the downward gift to its true giver.

luna: The section names عَذْب as pleasant fresh water beside عَذَاب; this ayah says God could make drinking water bitter-salty (أُجَاجًا) and asks why people are not grateful, making drinkable rain a bounded provision. | terra: God could make the water bitter, so drinkable sweetness is a contingent mercy rather than an entitlement.

luna: The section's dictionary note makes rain the life of dead earth; this ayah states the image's resulting claim directly, that God gives life to the earth after its death (يُحْيِى ٱلْأَرْضَ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا). | terra: God's revival of earth after its death is presented as a clarified sign, retaining the rain-resurrection conclusion even though water is implicit here.
terra: Worldly rivalry in increase is paired with rain whose growth delights, then withers and becomes debris; numerical swelling and water-fed transience share one image.
terra: Wealth and children are a trial, directly classifying material increase as testing rather than proof of honor.
terra: Unexpected provision, trust in God's sufficiency, and قَدْ جَعَلَ ٱللَّهُ لِكُلِّ شَىْءٍ قَدْرًا join rizq with a divinely set measure for everything.
terra: The well-provided spends from abundance and the one whose provision is restricted spends from what God gave; restriction is followed by promised ease, not humiliation.
terra: The creation of the Merciful contains no disparity, and the observer is challenged to find a fissure; this is the ordered boundary opposite fasād as departure from balance.
terra: Repeated looking returns unable to find a flaw, reinforcing created order as the background against which human corruption is imbalance.

luna: The section follows water emerging through earth and treats measured water as provision; this ayah asks who could bring flowing water if it sank into the ground (مَآءُكُمْ غَوْرًا), exposing how easily that provision could be hidden. | terra: If water sinks away, no one besides God can bring flowing water; the hidden-source scene reverses confident possession of provision.
terra: The garden owners are explicitly tested as they resolve to harvest, making a fruitful garden itself the form of trial.
terra: A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while its owners sleep, showing provision withdrawn outside their control.
terra: By morning the garden is like a field already reaped, the sudden loss reversing its expected fruitfulness.
terra: The owners finally say they have been deprived, voicing the human perception of narrowed provision after the garden vanishes.
terra: The garden owners finally glorify their Lord and confess wrongdoing, showing the moral recognition produced by deprivation.
terra: They confess إِنَّا كُنَّا طَاغِينَ, naming their own moral overflow within the garden-and-provision test.
terra: The garden's loss is called a worldly punishment and the Hereafter's punishment greater, clarifying that deprivation here belongs to a moral narrative rather than an automatic status rule.
terra: ʿĀd is destroyed by a clamorous, furious wind, identifying the force hidden inside the cloud they called rain.
terra: The wind is imposed for seven nights and eight days and leaves people like hollow palm trunks, extending the destructive aftermath of the false rain expectation.

luna: The section names ط غ ي for water exceeding its measure; this ayah uses the same root directly of the floodwater (طَغَى ٱلْمَاءُ) and says God carried people in the running ship. | terra: إِنَّا لَمَّا طَغَا ٱلْمَاءُ uses the section's overflow word literally of floodwater and sets saving carriage within the very water that exceeded its bound.
terra: Noah commands his people to seek forgiveness, beginning a passage in which moral return opens earthly water and provision.

luna: Noah tells his people that repentance would bring abundant rain (يُرْسِلِ ٱلسَّمَاءَ عَلَيْكُم مِّدْرَارًا); beside the section's destructive flood, this gives the same rain a merciful outcome. | terra: The promised answer is abundant rain sent from heaven, directly supplying the merciful opposite of Noah's destructive flood.

luna: The section ties rain to gardens and provision; continuing Noah's promise, this ayah links rain with wealth, children, gardens and rivers (جَنَّٰتٍ وَيَجْعَل لَّكُمْ أَنْهَٰرًا). | terra: Rain is followed by wealth, children, gardens, and rivers, gathering water, increased provision, and janna in one promise.
terra: Noah's people are drowned because of their sins and then admitted to fire, concretely joining moral transgression to overwhelming water.
terra: Within the Noah setting, the feared offspring is described as فَاجِرًا كَفَّارًا, supplying the sin branch of the same root beside the flood narrative.
terra: Steadfastness on the path would bring abundant water, making water itself the concrete form of expanded provision.
terra: The abundant water of the preceding ayah is explicitly a test, matching the section's insistence that provision is trial rather than proof of honor.

luna: The section's named ف ج ر branch is launching oneself into sin; this ayah says a person wants to sin ahead of himself (لِيَفْجُرَ أَمَامَهُ), giving the moral sense as an act. | terra: بَلْ يُرِيدُ ٱلْإِنسَانُ لِيَفْجُرَ أَمَامَهُ pictures the human wanting to break forward into sin, closely matching the source dictionary sense of opening and launching into disobedience.
terra: The righteous drink a cup mixed with camphor, introducing the spring they cause to gush in 76:6.

luna: Where the section says the Quran gives its bursting spring to God's servants in the Garden, this ayah describes a spring (عَيْنًا) that those servants make gush as they wish (يُفَجِّرُونَهَا تَفْجِيرًا), placing the same act in a setting of divine reward rather than a sign demanded from a messenger. | terra: God's servants drink from a spring that يُفَجِّرُونَهَا تَفْجِيرًا, transferring the act of making water gush to the people admitted to divine provision.
terra: Patient servants are rewarded with a garden before the later drink and spring details, setting the home of 76:6's gushing water.
terra: Reclining in the garden, the rewarded see neither burning sun nor bitter cold, defining the temperate setting around its flowing drink.
terra: Garden shade hangs near and fruit is brought within reach, extending the water-grown abundance of the reward.
terra: Silver vessels and cups circulate among them, supplying the containers whose exact measure is stated in 76:16.
terra: Paradise vessels are measured with exact measure, placing qadar even within the scene of freely given drink.
terra: They receive a cup mixed with ginger, leading into the named spring of 76:18.
terra: A spring named Salsabīl supplies the later paradise-drink scene, extending the flowing source introduced at 76:6.
terra: Firm mountains and fresh water are placed together as earth's provision, echoing rock, stored water, and drinkable sweetness without using the source's exact root.

luna: The section's ص ب ب image is water poured from above; this ayah calls rain pouring water (مَآءً ثَجَّاجًا) from the clouds, followed by grain and gardens in 78:15–16. | terra: وَأَنزَلْنَا مِنَ ٱلْمُعْصِرَاتِ مَاءً ثَجَّاجًا gives the image of water pouring profusely from rainclouds.

luna: The section's poured rain leads to food; this ayah names grain (حَبًّا) brought forth from the rain scene begun in 78:14. | terra: The purpose of that poured water is to bring forth grain and vegetation, identifying abundance as provided food.

luna: The section's ج ن ن note connects the garden to dense plant growth; following rain and grain, this ayah names thick, intertwined gardens (جَنَّٰتٍ أَلْفَافًا). | terra: Dense gardens are the final product of the descending water, matching the section's movement from rain to flourishing janna.
terra: Hell is an abode for the transgressors, identifying whose deprivation of drink and boiling liquid are described in 78:24-25.
terra: The transgressors taste neither coolness nor drink in hell, a deprivation of the two mercies associated with water.
terra: Only boiling fluid and foul discharge answer that deprivation, making liquid itself a fitting punitive counterpart.

luna: Moses is again sent to Pharaoh, who has transgressed (إِنَّهُۥ طَغَىٰ); this repeated formulation makes the section's water-overflow sense of ṭ-gh-y audible in the ruler's excess. | terra: The command to approach Pharaoh is again grounded in إِنَّهُۥ طَغَىٰ, directly identifying his crime with the section's flood word.
terra: The person who transgressed is introduced with the same water-overflow root used of the past tyrants.
terra: That transgressor prefers the nearer life, specifying the mistaken valuation that also accompanies rejoicing in expanded provision.
terra: Hell is the transgressor's refuge, giving the consequence of exceeding the life-giving measure.
terra: The opposing person fears standing before the Lord and restrains the self from desire, giving the inward form of staying within bounds.
terra: The garden is the refuge of the self that did not overflow, completing a direct transgression-versus-janna structure.
terra: The command فَلْيَنظُرِ ٱلْإِنسَانُ إِلَىٰ طَعَامِهِ frames the pouring and splitting in 80:25-26 as a lesson about the food a human calls provision.

luna: The section contrasts punishment poured from above with rain poured for food; this ayah uses the same ص ب ب verb for water (صَبَبْنَا ٱلْمَاءَ صَبًّا), whose benefit appears in the following verses. | terra: أَنَّا صَبَبْنَا ٱلْمَاءَ صَبًّا uses the same pouring verb as the punishment in the section, but the object poured from above is merciful water.

luna: The section's water-benefit scene continues as God splits the earth open (شَقَقْنَا ٱلْأَرْضَ شَقًّا) after pouring water in 80:25; the next verses identify the food that grows from it. | terra: The earth is then split open emphatically, reversing the destructive downward pouring into soil opened for growth.

luna: After the section's rain poured and earth split in 80:25–26, this continuing list begins with grain (حَبًّا), a specific yield of the life-giving water. | terra: Grain is the first named growth brought out after water is poured and earth is split.

luna: The food list following the section's cited rain-and-split-earth pair names grapes (عِنَبًا), making the water's provision concrete. | terra: Grapes and fresh herbage extend the concrete produce of the opened, watered ground.

luna: The section's final ج ن ن dictionary note describes plant thickening; this continuing harvest list names dense gardens (حَدَائِقَ غُلْبًا), a close picture of that growth. | terra: Olive and date palm show the continuing conversion of poured water into lasting food-bearing plants.

luna: The section's rain is linked to growing food; in the continuation after 80:25–26 this ayah names olives and palms (زَيْتُونًا وَنَخْلًا) as further yield. | terra: وَحَدَائِقَ غُلْبًا names luxuriant gardens as the flourishing outcome toward which the section's final janna image moves.

luna: The section says measured rain yields food; the same post-rain list names fruit and pasture (فَاكِهَةً وَأَبًّا), extending provision to people and animals. | terra: Fruit and pasture complete the range of products brought from the watered earth.

luna: The section reads restricted رزق as the humanly visible side of measured rain; the preceding crop list ends by calling its yield provision for people and livestock (مَّتَاعًا لَّكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ). | terra: مَتَاعًا لَّكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ states that the whole rain-growth sequence is provision for humans and their livestock.
terra: At judgment the faces are those of ٱلْكَفَرَةُ ٱلْفَجَرَةُ, carrying the root's moral branch into the same surah that earlier pours water and grows food.

luna: The section names the ف ج ر root both for bursting water and for fujūr, opening into sin; at the judgment the seas themselves are burst open (ٱلْبِحَارُ فُجِّرَتْ), making that physical and moral wording meet. | terra: وَإِذَا ٱلْبِحَارُ فُجِّرَتْ expands the same bursting-open action from a spring or river to the seas at the final unmaking.

luna: The section explicitly gives ف ج ر the secondary moral sense of opening into sins; this ayah names the wicked (ٱلْفُجَّارَ) and sets their Fire against the righteous' bliss in the preceding ayah. | terra: The wicked are named ٱلْفُجَّارِ in the same surah whose seas are burst open at 82:3, letting the two Qur'anic branches of the root sound within one judgment scene.

luna: The section explicitly gives ف ج ر a moral sense; this ayah calls the wrongdoers al-fujjār (ٱلْفُجَّارِ) and places their record in Sijjīn, another concrete use of the named secondary sense. | terra: The record of the fujjār is placed in Sijjīn; this carries the developed sin sense of the root into a reckoning context parallel to surah 89.

luna: The section's lexicon says رَجْع can mean rain that falls, returns and falls again; this ayah swears by the sky of recurring return (وَٱلسَّمَآءِ ذَاتِ ٱلرَّجْعِ), giving that rain cycle a direct formulation. | terra: The oath by وَٱلسَّمَاءِ ذَاتِ ٱلرَّجْعِ supplies the source section's secondary sense of rajʿ as repeatedly returning rain beside the soul's commanded return.
luna: The section's rain-return image in 86:11 is followed by earth with a crack (وَٱلْأَرْضِ ذَاتِ ٱلصَّدْعِ), returning the reader to its opening image of a split through which water emerges.
terra: The Creator proportions what He creates, supplying the making-fit aspect of the section's measured water order.
terra: God determines and guides, pairing qadar with direction rather than with humiliation or arbitrary lack.
terra: The condemned are given drink from a fiercely hot spring, the direct punitive opposite of the flowing spring in the garden at 88:12.
terra: The rewarded person is in a high garden, supplying the setting for the flowing spring of 88:12.
terra: A flowing spring lies within the high garden, joining the section's water motion to its final destination.

luna: The section's named fujūr is the moral opening into sin; this ayah names the soul's wickedness (فُجُورَهَا) beside its godwariness (وَتَقْوَىٰهَا), clarifying the moral sense against its water-bursting sense. | terra: The soul is inspired with its fujūr and its taqwā, placing the source dictionary's “opening into sin” against an inward moral boundary.
terra: God's messenger names the she-camel and her drink as the boundary Thamūd must honor.
terra: They deny, hamstring the camel, and are crushed for their sin, showing destruction after violating the measured water arrangement.
terra: The human being is declared prone to transgress, beginning the exact diagnosis of abundance misread as self-sufficiency.
terra: The reason given is that the human sees himself self-sufficient, closely explaining why expanded provision can become overflow.

luna: The section names divine honoring and provision before the surah corrects the wealthy person's claim; this ayah identifies pushing away the orphan (يَدُعُّ ٱلْيَتِيمَ) as the contrary human measure of honor.

luna: The section's abundance-and-restriction test turns on what people do with provision; this ayah rebukes failing to urge food for the needy (طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ), giving the social consequence of misreading wealth as honor.
